the role of WM in the integration of words in the context of spoken language.
the effects of individual differences on the neural processing of discourse.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
high WM individuals are more sensitive to discourse congruence, but less sensitive to local word associations.
WM capacity is associated with both the processing of lexical associations and the processing of discourse congruency.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ability to suppress task-irrelevant information is related to the ability to process discourse context, but that the ability to process context is related to the amount of WM capacity.

WM capacity affects the processing of discourse structure and lexical association, with high WM capacity individuals relying more on top-down processes and low capacity individuals relying more heavily on the lexical associations between words.
WM capacity and the cognitive processes associated with it affect both the local processing and integration of individual words into the discourse representation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
individual differences in WM capacity affect the processing of local lexical association information and global discourse congruency information in discourse comprehension.
WM is related to the processing of both local and global discourse congruency.
individual variability in WM capacity and cognitive control can affect how people process the local associations and discourse congruence of words when they are listening to spoken discourse.
